title: Melania Trump says she helped another group of children return to Ukraine. The reality is more complicated
summary: Nine children and a 29-year-old woman with disabilites returned to Ukraine on Friday via Belarus, part of a reunification mission to unite families separated by Russia's war with Ukraine.

image.caption: Alina Sydorenko sees her son, Artem, 8, for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022. He arrived in Ukraine with eight other children from Belarus on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

blocks.text: When Alina Sydorenko woke up last week and discovered that drones and missiles had dealt a devastating blow to Russia's prized Kerch Bridge — causing a central section to collapse — it was the first time she felt annoyed by a Ukrainian win in the war against Russia.

Her mother was planning to cross the bridge from occupied Crimea into Russia to escort Sydorenko's eight-year-old son, Artem, out of their home in the southeastern port city of Berdyansk, which Russian troops seized during the early days of the war against Ukraine.
Sydorenko was in northern Ukraine when the full-scale invasion began in February 2022 and said she was separated from her only child for years.

items: There can be no peace with Russia until Ukrainian children come home, says advocate

blocks.text: While Ukraine says it has confirmed more than 20,000 cases of children being deported or forcibly transferred to Russia, thousands of others remain separated by the war — either trapped in occupied territory or in Russia because the relatives they were with at the start of the invasion fled there.
"The negotiations took a very long time," Sydorenko said in an interview with CBC News on Friday at a Ukrainian checkpoint a few kilometres from the border with Belarus.
"I can't even say how much stress and effort we went through to bring the child back here. It's terrifying to worry every single day about whether they are alive."

Artem and his grandmother ended up waiting a few days before taking a train to Russia. From there, they joined a larger group and travelled through Belarus as part of a humanitarian reunification mission secured in part with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who met with Melania in Washington, D.C. after she was credited with securing a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied community of Oleshky, even went so far as to say she is now their chief mediator when it comes to the return of children.
Families separated by war reunite at Ukraine-Belarus border
Politics, public pressure play role in return

Before starting the long journey to reunite with their children, families face a mountain of paperwork and permissions. However, politics and public pressure are also factoring into how and when some of those who have been separated or forcibly deported to Russia are brought back to Ukraine.
The group that arrived on Friday included nine children and 29-year-old Anastasia (Nastia) Mamotiuk, who lives with a disability and has been in institutional group care since she was a young child.

items: 'We need strong support': Ukraine fighting to bring children back from Russia

blocks.text: She was one of more than 80 children and vulnerable young adults taken to Russia from the Oleshky Children’s Boarding School in southern Ukraine in the fall of 2022.

In recent months, the Emile Foundation, a humanitarian organization with offices in the Netherlands and Ukraine, has been able to track down more than 40 of the school's former residents. Bringing them back to Ukraine has been challenging due to medical needs, legal hurdles and the difficulty of locating individuals in the first place — especially as some have been shuffled between different care facilities.
Anastasia (Nastia) Mamotiuk, 29, arrives by ambulance at the Ukraine-Belarus border checkpoint on Friday. She had been placed at a facility in Russia. (Nicolas Hameon/CBC)
The foundation made contact with Mamotiuk in the spring and kept in touch on WhatsApp through messages and video calls.

"We were in touch with her all the time," said Mariam Lambert, co-founder and CEO of the Emile Foundation, who spoke to CBC News via Zoom. "There were good moments, there were really bad moments, there were moments where she was scared."

items: Ukrainian children abducted by Russia appeal for help from Canadian MPs

blocks.text: Mamotiuk was placed in a facility in Penza, Russia, a city about 500 kilometres southeast of Moscow. The home was managed by Sofia Lvova-Belova, the sister of Russia's children's commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court and accused of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children to Russia.
Lambert said it was during their regular communication with Mamotiuk in May that she began expressing concern about being given more medication than she typically took.
A boy looks out from a bus transporting children from Belarus back to Ukraine on Friday. The children have been living away from home because of war with Russia. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

Then in the fall, she suddenly stopped communicating with those in Ukraine for several days. That prompted Lambert to go public with Mamotiuk’s case, speaking to the media and appealing to Melania Trump to intervene.
"We understand the political side of it, and this is why we made an appeal," Lambert said. "We were asking, of course, the international community to put pressure on Russia in order to return her."

items: Melania Trump hosted officials from Russia and Ukraine. Just what's behind her peace push?

blocks.text: A few days later, Mamotiuk was back in touch and was told arrangements were being made to get her a passport so she could travel.
CBC News reached out to the office of Russia’s children’s commissioner but has not received a response.
'Is it becoming a political game?'

While Lambert praised the International Committee of the Red Cross for helping arrange Mamotiuk's travel, she was dismayed by how much of her return to Ukraine unfolded. She said they first heard about the reunification from Melania, who posted about it on social media on Nov. 25.
In a press release, the White House stated that the latest agreement meant 43 children had now been "reunited through her humanitarian efforts."

The statement made it seem as though the children were already back with relatives, when in reality they were still in transit and had not yet reached Belarus — which they needed to pass through in order to cross into northern Ukraine.

Olha, right, who didn't want her last name published because of the high profile and sensitivity of the humanitarian mission in the midst of war, reunited with her nephew, Sasha. He had been living in occupied Kherson with his mother. When she died four months ago, he asked if he could leave and relocate to Kyiv to live with his aunt. (Briar Stewart/CBC)
After the announcement, the first lady reposted U.S. coverage of the reunification interspersed with posts promoting a new docuseries about her that's streaming on Amazon Prime.
Lambert only found out that Mamotiuk was arriving on Friday when the young woman got in touch herself.
"Is it really a humanitarian action, or is it becoming a political game?" she said.
Alevtyna Abibulaieva, left, kisses her niece, Valeriia Levchenko, 11, who crossed the border into Ukraine from Belarus by bus on Friday. (Evgeniy Maloletka/The Associated Press)
Bus arrives to waiting family, officials, media
Because they are not directly related, no one from the Emile Foundation was invited to the border checkpoint to welcome Mamotiuk — and neither was her closest contact, Viacheslav Shchyrskyi.

The 61-year-old had been in touch with Mamotiuk for more than a decade. He previously ran a small group home in Ukraine's Kherson region and was making arrangements to take her in before the war. But all of the legal paperwork was shelved after Russia's full-scale invasion began.

items: Russia is accused of deporting thousands of Ukrainian children. 17 returned home this week

blocks.text: Shchyrskyi told CBC News that he spoke to Mamotiuk at the border as she was leaving Belarus.

"Finally, she's got what she wanted. She's been brought to Ukraine, but she's confused," he said in a phone interview with CBC News from Romania, where he currently lives. "Even though she's 29 years old, deep down she's still a child — a little girl who has been moved from one place to another, and then moved again."
The Emile Foundation's Maria Lebedieva, seen on a cellphone screen, speaks with Mamotiuk near the border checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

As the bus carrying the children arrived at the checkpoint on Friday afternoon, relatives, Ukrainian officials and a crush of cameras rushed toward the opening doors. Off to the side, an ambulance pulled up carrying Mamotiuk.
When CBC News entered the vehicle to greet her, she lay on a stretcher staring at the ceiling. She appeared quiet and unsure.

items: 'They wanted children': Ukrainian doctors say they lied to keep kids safe from Russian troops

blocks.text: When we asked if she wanted to say hello to Maria Lebedieva, director of the Emile Foundation's Ukraine branch, who was waiting on the other side of the secured checkpoint, Mamotiuk's mood lifted.
Seeing a friendly face on a video call, a smile spread across her face. She said she hoped to see Lebedieva soon and wanted to know when she could see Shchyrskyi.
Sydorenko tightly hugs her son Artem after being reunited at a checkpoint about five kilometres from the Ukraine-Belarus border on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)
Outside of the ambulance, some children got back on the bus with their relatives, while others, like Artem, got into vehicles to make the onward journey.
"I am even happier than I thought I would be," Sydorenko said as she prepared to leave with her son and head back to Kyiv.
As for Mamotiuk, a Ukrainian flag was placed over her legs like a blanket just before the ambulance carrying her pulled away toward a medical facility south of the capital.
